lesson.title: Far From the Center: Understanding Leverage
lesson.summary: Leverage measures how far a point's x-value sits from the mean of x, and high leverage gives a point the potential, though not the guarantee, to be influential.
lesson.body:
An influential point, as we just saw, can drag a regression line toward it hard enough to reverse its slope. But what actually gives a point that kind of power? The answer is leverage, a measure of how far a point's x-value is from the mean of all the x-values in the data set. Points near the center of the x-values have low leverage, because the line is anchored by the bulk of the data around it and one central point can't tip the balance much. Points far out on the x-axis, in either direction, have high leverage, because they sit at the end of a long lever arm and even a modest shift in that point can rotate the whole line noticeably, the same way pushing on the end of a long seesaw plank moves it more than pushing near the middle.

Go back to the six-student data set from influential points: five students with hours studied from 1 to 5, plus a sixth who studied 20 hours. The mean of all six x-values is 35/6, about 5.83. The added student's x-value, 20, is 14.17 units away from that mean, dramatically farther than any of the other five points, which sit between 0.83 and 4.83 units from the mean. That distance is exactly why this point had the power to flip the slope: it was the farthest point from the center of the x-values by a wide margin, and leverage cares only about that horizontal distance, not about what the student's score happened to be.

Leverage can be quantified precisely. For simple linear regression, the leverage of point i is h_i = 1/n + (x_i - x-bar)-squared / Sxx, where Sxx is the sum of squared deviations of x from its mean. Using the six-point data set, Sxx works out to about 250.83. For the added student, x = 20: h = 1/6 + (20 - 5.83)-squared / 250.83 = 0.167 + 200.7/250.83 = 0.167 + 0.800 = 0.967, a leverage value extremely close to the maximum possible value of 1. For a student near the center, x = 3: h = 1/6 + (3 - 5.83)-squared / 250.83 = 0.167 + 8.03/250.83 = 0.167 + 0.032 = 0.199, a much smaller value. This formula is background enrichment rather than something tested directly, but the pattern it produces, leverage growing as a point's x moves away from the mean, is the core idea to remember. As a rough rule of thumb used in some introductory treatments, a leverage value above about 4/n (here, 4/6, or 0.667) is worth a second look; the added student's leverage of 0.967 clears that bar easily, while the student at x = 3, with leverage 0.199, does not.

High leverage is a warning sign, not a verdict. A high-leverage point that happens to fall right on the trend the rest of the data follows will barely change the line at all if removed, because its y-value was exactly what the pattern predicted anyway. It only becomes influential, in the sense studied under influential points, when high leverage is combined with a y-value that breaks from that pattern. Leverage describes potential energy; whether that potential is ever spent bending the line depends on where the point actually falls. This is precisely the distinction that separates leverage from the related idea of a regression outlier, which is about an unusual y-value rather than an unusual x-value, and which is examined next.
